name: HireKey
tagline: Your recruiter-informed AI copilot for tech job search
description: HireKey is a recruiter-informed AI job-search co-pilot for tech job seekers who want to apply strategically & interview with confidence. It helps you assess your role fit, tailor resumes, communicate experience & track applications. Unlike basic ATS tools, HireKey combines AI with 10 years of recruiting experience at Microsoft, Amazon & Stripe, plus practice out loud with an interactive AI voice coach that responds to your answers & provides real-time interview feedback.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt! 👋

I’m Nela, co-founder of HireKey

I spent 10 years recruiting for technical and non-technical roles at Microsoft, Amazon, and Stripe, to name a few. I reviewed thousands of resumes and interviewed thousands of candidates.

Time and time again, I saw qualified people get passed over simply because their resumes didn’t connect their experience to the role, or because they struggled to explain that experience in an interview. They had the right skills, but hiring managers weren’t seeing the connection.

That stayed with me because many of those people were incredibly talented, genuine people whom I had to give the unfortunate news of rejection, which is honestly the worst part of recruiting.

So, we built HireKey around the recruiting knowledge I’d gathered over those 10 years, giving job seekers access to the perspective from the other side of the hiring table.

HireKey helps you assess how your experience fits a role, tailor your resume, practice interviews with an interactive AI voice coach, and track your applications in one place.

How it works

1. Add the job and your master resume. Find a role you want to apply for and add its title, company, location, and job description to HireKey’s Job Tracker. Upload your master resume once, then use it across the jobs you’re considering.

2. Tailor your resume and assess your fit. HireKey adapts your master resume to the job description, bringing your relevant experience into focus, along with an analysis of missing skills or experience and whether transferable experience could help bridge those gaps.

3. Practice out loud, on demand. Practice using the STAR framework with an interactive AI voice coach. Get specific feedback on where your answers are strongest and where you still need practice.

4. Keep your search organized. Track applications through stages such as applied, screening, and interviewing, so you always know where things stand.

Coming soon: Chrome extension for auto job capture
Premium users will be able to use a chrome extension that will automatically capture job details and enter them into HireKey's job tracker

A closer look at interview practice

Knowing your work and explaining it clearly are two different skills. This was something I saw repeatedly as a recruiter, and it’s why interview practice is such an important part of HireKey.

You can choose practice questions or add your own, then start speaking with the coach, all on demand. It responds to what you actually say and helps you identify where an answer needs more clarity or detail. You also get a debrief on what went well and what to improve.

Prefer to prepare on your own first? You can print interview questions with tips on how to approach your answers.

Who it’s for

HireKey is built for people pursuing technical and non-technical roles in tech, especially when you:

- Find an interesting role but aren’t sure how well your experience fits.
- Need help making your relevant experience clear on your resume.
- Know your work but struggle to explain it in an interview.
- Have multiple applications in progress and need to keep track of them.

Get 1 month of Premium free with our Product Hunt launch offer.

We’d love to hear from you: What’s hardest about job searching? Is it deciding where to apply, showing your experience on paper, or talking about it in an interview?

name: kōdlo
tagline: End-to-end sales workspace with unified context
description: kōdlo finds prospects that fit your ICP and tells you how to warm each one up. Upload product catalogues and other docs to the Knowledge Hub, and its agent turns them into personalized messages, offers, deep searches and decks. Track client data, collaborate with your team, and manage tasks, all in one place. Connect Claude Desktop/ChatGPT Work or your code agent with kōdlo MCP to scale and orchestrate contexts.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt 👋 Andriana here, co-founder of kōdlo🐍

The Problem. Selling a complex product takes hours of prep. You jump between a few disconnected tools to research accounts, draft personalized outreach, and assemble pitch decks. Context gets lost, and you end up spending more time on prep than talking to buyers.

The Solution. kōdlo is an end-to-end sales workspace that keeps the context for you. Find prospects, research them, and write messages, proposals and decks in one place. Everything you do there, from research and notes to your documents and past conversations, stays in kōdlo's memory, so each new piece of work builds on what it already knows.

What makes it different? kōdlo is built on one shared memory that every agent can use. The agent also sees what you see. Chat sits on the left, your work on the right. On top of that sits everything you need to sell: prospecting, research, your own knowledge base, outreach, decks, a task tracker, team collaboration and scheduled work.

Key features:
🎯 Find prospects with a reason. Describe who you sell to and kōdlo finds matching companies and decision makers. Each one comes with evidence for why it fits, like a funding round, a job ad or a line on their website.
🔍 Deep search. Research on any company, market or person, written up as a report where every claim links to its source.
📚 Knowledge Hub. Upload price lists, case studies, tech docs, even scanned PDFs. kōdlo answers from your own documents and cites the file and page it used.
✍️ Writes in your voice. LinkedIn messages, connection notes and proposals in a tone of voice you set once. You send them yourself.
📊 Decks in your brand. kōdlo builds a template from your PowerPoint and exports to PPTX or PDF.
⏰ Work that keeps going. Put tasks on a schedule or hand kōdlo a list of up to 5,000 rows to work through.
🔌 Your context in your AI tools. Connect kōdlo over MCP and use the same prospects, plans, documents and decks in Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex, OpenAI Work and Dots, or any other tool that supports MCP.



Who is it for? Founders and small teams selling B2B SaaS, sales people in IT services companies, and anyone selling a technical product where the know-how sits with the engineers.

🎬 Interactive demo → https://app.arcade.software/share/qlAB1iPeVNpCtpgd2yL9
🎁 PH offer → The first 100 sign-ups get 10% off the Starter plan.

Huge thanks to our core team, Ivan, Jakub and Vitalii, and to Rohan for hunting us!
We’re here for honest feedback and our first users. Tell us what works, what feels confusing, and what’s missing — we’re ready for critiques. Every comment gets read, and the best ideas go straight onto our roadmap.

name: OpenScreen 2
tagline: Record your demo and let your AI agent do the edits
description: Record your screen and the demo looks great on the first take: zooms planned from your clicks, smooth cursor, 3D camera moves, cursor themes, backgrounds and webcam layouts. Then let your AI agent do the edit over MCP, or cut the video yourself by deleting words in the transcript. Windows, macOS and Linux. Free, MIT, no account, no watermark.

nodes.body:
Hi Product Hunt, I'm Etienne and I maintain OpenScreen.

It started as Siddharth Vaddem's side project, a free alternative to Screen Studio. He archived it in June and I took it over with his approval. 2.0 is four months of work since then, and 137 people have contributed to the project so far.

What's new:

  • a local MCP server, so Claude Code or another agent can do the edit for you

  • zooms planned from your clicks, as shots, not one per click

  • cut the video by deleting words in the transcript, captions transcribed locally

  • webcam beside or above the recording, with background blur or removal

  • a native GPU renderer, exports about 15x faster than before on our reference laptop

  • a 3D camera that moves with your zooms, and five cursor themes with sculpted 3D versions

Windows, macOS and Linux. Free and MIT, no account, no watermark. Thanks to Siddharth for starting it, and to everyone who contributes.

What do you make your demos with today, and what would OpenScreen need for you to switch?

Congrats Etienne, and good on you for picking it up instead of letting it sit archived.

I went through the OpenScreen source a while back. The comment in zoomSpring.ts about the eased target causing a jerk at zoom seams changed how I think about camera motion. Small detail, but you can feel it in the result.

Curious about "zooms as shots": how do you decide which clicks go in one shot? Time gap, distance on screen, or both?
Congratulation! I use Screen Studio a while, then switched to Record, now, I I'd like to try OpenScreen!

free, MIT, no watermark on a tool this polished is rare, respect for keeping it that way through the rewrite. question on the transcript-based cutting: local transcription is never perfect, so what happens when the agent deletes a word that got misheard and the cut lands mid-sentence instead of in the pause? does it show you the edit list before committing, or is undo the main safety net there?
I like that it works on Windows, Mac, and Linux. No accounts or watermark is a nice bonus too.

name: Ayven
tagline: Carries and drives your team's agenda
description: Ayven drives your agenda. It means observing, cutting the work into pieces your team can take one at a time, putting an owner and a date on each, and filing them in Jira or YouTrack. Then it runs, tracks and talks about the work for weeks: asking whoever knows, waiting, chasing silence, moving work when someone is away. Your team answers in Slack and the board moves. Planning stops being the barrier and you ship your agenda like crazy.

nodes.body:
Howard here, founder of Alknoma.

We didn't start with a product. We started with an ANNOYANCE. Agents were impressive while you were talking to them, and then, as soon as you stopped typing, they effectively disappeared.

You'd put one in Slack and end up with another bot sitting in a channel waiting for someone to tell it what to do.

You don't prompt your teammates.


So the real problem was never, "How do we make the model smarter?" It was: how do you give a language model a spine? Something that lets it chain call after call, across days and months, reaching out to different people, all without a human babysitting it.

Sounds impossible if you know from experience just how complex chaining LLM calls can be. Three things turned out to matter, and we learned each one the painful way.


1. What a piece of work actually is.

Small enough that it can be validated, iterated, executed and closed 99.9% of the time.

Too big and the agent starts hallucinating. Too small and it loses all semantic meaning.


2. Resolving time should be first-class.

A lot of work in a team is essentially waiting.

Waiting isn't failure. It's the norm. And that happens to be one of the things LLM agents are worst at. Ayven reasons about when it should wake up next, EVERY SINGLE TIME, across thousands of runs a week.

It is about recognising a deadline, annual leave, or when a teammate has gone quiet. The async gap is hard to nail down. Ayven does that.


3. What is the base unit of a fact.

In a team, things change constantly. Someone changes their mind, a deadline moves, a customer replies, a meeting gets cancelled. An agent would treat information that was true two days ago as gospel. Change is the critical signal, and that was difficult to implement when teamwork is so unpredictable. Ayven makes sure the right things change with it.


The magic moment that wowed us, and made us decide to launch Ayven: we gave Ayven the agenda for September. Nothing else. The next thing we knew, the board was full, and accurate to our plans. It put together the pieces of what execution would look like.

Later, I asked: "What's stopping us from launching on Product Hunt?" Ayven then told me about every dependencies that I did not previously know. Nobody wrote that answer. It was just the work being captured in its truest, current state.

There is a lot more to Ayven that we haven't covered here.

Talk to us if you want this deployed in your own environment. Tell us what you want it connected to.

Ask me anything :)

name: Foley
tagline: A voice to-do list that files, plans and asks first
description: Say what needs doing. Foley turns it into a task with the project, date and reminder already set, and asks when it isn't sure instead of guessing. When plans change, say so and it moves the task. Ask it to plan your day, or what to work on first, and it answers from your list. Capture from your Apple Watch. The desktop app is free with no account, using your own OpenRouter key. Foley Pro runs the AI for you and syncs every device. On iPhone, Android, Mac, Windows and the web.

nodes.body: Hi Product Hunt. I'm José, a software engineer with over 25 years of experience (https://www.linkedin.com/in/jose...). I kept losing tasks I said out loud: mid-meeting, in the car, walking the dog. Foley is the to-do list I wanted for that. You talk, and it files. It handles time the way people say it ("next Tuesday morning"), and it asks when it isn't sure instead of guessing. When plans change, say so and it moves the task. Ask it to plan your day, or what to work on first, and it answers from your own list. The desktop app is free with no account, using your own OpenRouter key. Foley Pro is $8 a month on the web, and your first month there is $4, applied at checkout. I'll be here all day. Tell me what it got wrong.
Will grab TestFlight this week — the ambiguous follow-up is exactly what I need when a voice note is just "sort the invoices" with no folder named.
FYI, hello@foleyapp.com bounces with a 550 from Google Workspace

Voice is the future!

The UI is very clean (dark mode reins supreme though)
When you ask it to plan your day, does it order tasks by the reminders already attached, or does it decide priority on its own? I'd want it to lean on the dates I already gave it rather than guess.
Congrats on the launch. I like that it asks before filing — half my voice dumps are just "call them back" with zero context. Does the clarifying step happen on-device or after sync?
can the created tasks also be synced to desire PM tools like clickup
Using an Apple Watch to capture tasks is a nice touch. Sometimes pulling out your phone is already too much friction.
Finally an assistant can help organize the chaos in my head without making me type everything out.
can it handle task well even when plans change?

Handling relative time like "next Tuesday morning" is the part of voice capture that usually breaks first. Building voice AI for older adults, the trickiest case for us was self-corrections mid-sentence ("Thursday, no wait, Friday"). Does Foley treat the last thing said as the final intent, or does it ask you to confirm when it hears a correction like that?

"asks when it isn't sure instead of guessing" is the right default and most voice products get it backwards because asking feels like friction and guessing feels like magic, until the guess is wrong and now you've got a task filed under the wrong project with a made-up date. we fight the same tradeoff on calls at Dial. where's the line for you on what counts as "not sure", confidence score under some threshold, or ambiguity between two specific candidates like two projects with similar names?

name: Gboard Kurukuru Version
tagline: Your fingers stay put. The keys come around
description: Gboard Kurukuru Version is a conveyor belt keyboard from Google Japan's Gboard team, its 15th. Four belts carry 29 keys each past your fingers, so one hand can reach every character. It isn't for sale, but STL files, firmware and a build guide are on GitHub.

nodes.body:
Hi everyone!

Google Japan's Gboard team keeps coming up with wonderfully odd keyboard ideas, and it has become a yearly tradition. This is the 15th, after a one-key Morse keyboard, a teacup, a rotary phone and a hat.

This year's is the Gboard Conveyor Belt Version in the repo, and くるくる in Japanese. Kurukuru is the sound of something going round and round, which is what the keys do. Four belts carry 29 keys each, 116 in total, and the letter you want comes around to your fingers. Upper and lower case are both on the belts, and one hand is enough for everything.

You can also build it. The build guide covers the 3D-printed frame, an N20 motor and Choc low-profile switches, with KiCad board files and firmware in the same repo. The keycaps in the parts list are blank, so what goes on them is up to you!

I love that Google still spends time building things like this haha. Is it practical? Probably not. Would I love to try it? Absolutely. Curious how long it would actually take to type a full sentence compared to a regular keyboard.
wtf
What a delightfully clever twist bringing the keys to your fingers instead of moving your fingers to the keys, and open-sourcing the whole build makes it even better.
the conveyor belt idea is smart and makes typing in diffrent languages much easier

name: Edgee Mod for Claude Code
tagline: Use any model inside Claude Code, keep your Claude plan
description: A Claude Code mod that puts Edgee in your terminal. Keep your Claude plan, switch your session to any of 200+ models in one keystroke, and see live what compression and routing save you. Same conversation, same context. Two commands to install.

nodes.body: Hey Product Hunt 👋 Sacha here, CEO of Edgee. Like a lot of you, we spend our days in Claude Code, on a Claude plan. It's great. But some tasks deserve another model: a cheaper one for routine work, a specialized coder, or the new model everyone is talking about this week. Until now, trying one meant leaving your session and losing your context. So we built the Edgee Mod for Claude Code. It uses Claude Code's new mods system, so it runs inside Claude Code itself: 🔀 Switch models in one keystroke. Open the Edgee panel, search 200+ models, press Enter. The next request goes to that model, in the same conversation. One click on "Claude Code's choice" and you're back on your plan. 💸 See what you save. Folded, it's a single line above your prompt. Getting started takes two commands: curl -fsSL https://edgee.ai/install.sh | bash edgee launch claude Fun timing: Mistral Large 4 just came out and it's already available in Edgee. congrats on the launch!

different angle from the compression thread, two quick ones.

requests go through your gateway so whats retained? i work on a product where customer data cant leave the tenant, and someone always has to answer 'where did the code go' before we adopt anything.. self host, or logging you can turn off??

also, when a request routes to another model mid conversation there's no warm prefix on that side, so that call should be expensive. does the savings donut account for it?

(btw i'm not AI 😂)

switching models mid-conversation and keeping "same context" is the part I'd want to pressure-test. compression is probably fine for prose, but code context is unforgiving - a dropped variable name or a compressed-away line of a diff doesn't just lose nuance, it can make the next model's edit wrong in a way that's hard to notice until it breaks. is the compression ratio different for code blocks versus natural language in the conversation, or does it treat the whole context the same way?
Congrats on your launch! 🚀

nodes.body: Hi Product Hunt, I'm Ökte, the maker of Agibot. Most AI assistants only work while you're chatting with them. Close the tab and they stop. I wanted one that keeps going in the background and checks in with me when it matters. That's Agibot: an always-on personal AI agent that runs on your own computer. What it does - Keeps working in the background, even after you close the window - Sends you updates on a schedule, like a morning brief - Keeps an eye on things and only messages you when something changes - Handles tasks on the web for you, and on Mac it can use your apps too - Talks with you in the app, on Telegram or on Slack, in one shared conversation Why you can trust it - It asks before doing anything risky, and you decide what it can do on its own - Your chats and memories are saved on your computer - You can see, edit and delete everything it remembers - One click stops everything It gets better as you use it Correct it once, like "keep my briefs to five lines", and it remembers next time. What it costs Free forever with your own API key. Use OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and others, or run a free local model. You pay the AI provider directly, with nothing added on top. Join the waitlist for Mac, with Windows next. I'll be here in the comments all day. What would you hand off to it first? https://agibot.sh

It seems like Agibot makes sense for people who don’t want to run their AI agent in the cloud, but for everyone else, wouldn’t Grok bot or dots be a better choice? Does Agibot have any advantages over those alternatives?

"asks before doing anything risky" is doing a lot of work in that sentence and it's the part I'd actually want to understand before trusting an always-on agent with my own API key running unattended. is "risky" a fixed list you ship with, deleting files, sending messages, spending money, or something the agent itself judges case by case? a fixed list is auditable but will miss things, a judgment call is more flexible but means the bar moves depending on how the model is feeling that day.

name: SimpleSpread
tagline: Native, open source Mac spreadsheet
description: Ever double click a CSV or XLSX file on your mac and have to wait 30 seconds while Numbers loads? And when it loads it's filled with a ton of crap you don't need? Then I wrote this for you (well mostly me, but you might find it cool too). A small, fast spreadsheet for the Mac, written entirely in Swift. Free and MIT open source with XLSX as the native file format. 156 functions, incremental recalc, Excel-style keyboard editing.

nodes.body:
Hi Everyone,

I wanted a spreadsheet on my Mac that opens fast, edits an .xlsx file and saves it back, and does nothing else. Numbers converts everything into its own format. Excel is a subscription and a big install for opening a CSV. Google Sheets wants a browser and an account.

So I built SimpleSpread. It is a native Mac app, written entirely in Swift, and the whole spreadsheet stack is from scratch: the model, the formula engine, the XLSX reader and writer (down to the ZIP layer), CSV and the grid. The only outside library is Sparkle, for updates.

• XLSX is the native format. Open a file from Excel, Numbers or Google Sheets, edit it, save it, send it back. Styles, number formats, formulas with cached values, merged ranges and frozen panes all survive the round trip.
• CSV done properly: delimiter sniffing, BOM and CP1252 detection, leading zeros kept, and a field like =cmd imports as text, never as a formula.
• 156 functions with the coercion rules Sheets and Excel share: SUMIFS with wildcards, XLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH, IRR/XIRR, dates and text. Incremental recalc and cycle detection.
• It edits like Excel: Enter/Edit modes, type to replace, F2, ⌘-arrow jumps, fill handle, ⌘D / ⌘R, real undo, Find, zoom.
• Notarized, and it updates itself in place.

Upfront about what it is not: no charts, no pivot tables, no conditional formatting, no array formulas, no INDIRECT/OFFSET yet, and no collaboration. Frozen panes and merged cells are kept in the file but not drawn yet. It is Apple Silicon only, macOS 14 or later, and en-US number and date input for now.

It's free, MIT licensed and on GitHub, so read it, fork it, send patches. I'd love to hear which missing feature stops you using it day to day. Find & Replace and Paste Values are next on my list.
Clean, silicon-native version of bloated software that still uses the same filetype? Yes.

the CSV formula-injection detail ("=cmd" importing as text, never as a formula) is the kind of thing most hobby spreadsheet projects never even think about, let alone fix on purpose. that's a real security corner most people only learn about after getting bitten. also shipping pivot tables an hour after someone said that's what would stop them using it is a pretty wild turnaround, were they half-built already or did you actually just go build that from the comment?
no pivot tables would stop me honestly, i lean on those way more than charts for quick totals

name: Kooler
tagline: Find cocktails you can make with what's in your bar
description: Kooler is a free cocktail recipe app for people who like making drinks at home. - My Bar: add the bottles and ingredients you have and see every drink you can make right now - 100+ curated recipes: classics, modern cocktails and Brazilian drinks like Caipirinha, Rabo de Galo and Macunaíma - Clear measurements, step-by-step methods and consistent photos - Check-ins: rate a drink you had at a bar and share it No ads, no paywall. Web + iOS.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt! I'm Edu, a product designer from São Paulo.

Kooler is actually a comeback. A friend and I built the first version back in 2010: a little social network for cocktail recipes, with one feature we loved — tell it what you have at home and it shows what you can make. In 2011 I moved to São Paulo for a new job and we shut it down.

Fifteen years later I rebuilt it. I'm a designer, not a developer, so this time I built it with AI tools, from the database to the iOS app.

What's in it:
- My Bar: add what's in your cabinet and see every drink you can make
- 100+ curated recipes, from the classics to Brazilian drinks most cocktail apps skip (Rabo de Galo, Macunaíma, Caju Amigo)
- Clean recipe pages with clear measurements and consistent photos
- Check-ins to rate a drink you had at a bar

It's free, with no ads. Recipe submissions from the community are next.

I'd love your feedback: what's missing, what's confusing, and which drink you'd look up first. 🍸
Coming back to something you built 15 years ago says a lot. And a designer building the whole thing, database to iOS app, is pretty inspiring. Congrats Edu...

the my-bar matching is the feature that actually gets used daily, most cocktail apps assume you'll just go buy the one missing ingredient and quietly become a shopping list app instead. curious about the edge case though: when a recipe needs something close to what's already in my bar but not exact, a different vermouth, gin instead of a specific bitters, does it ever surface a "one swap away" match, or is the matching strict on exact ingredients only? that's the difference between "here's what's technically in your bar" and "here's what you're actually drinking tonight." rebuilding this 15 years later as a solo designer with AI tools is a good story too, the first version clearly left a mark if you came back to it.
Not every home bartender wants complicated recipes with 15 ingredients. Simple classics would be my go-to here.
I am not a beverage sommelier, but the platform looks pretty elegant!

name: Unboom
tagline: Tames boomy room bass on your Mac without acoustic panels
description: Unboom finds the bass note your untreated room exaggerates and gently turns just that down on your Mac. Scan with your mic or pick it by ear, choose Gentle, Medium, or Strong, and flip Correction on. Never boosts. No data collected. No subscription.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt 👋

If you make music with studio monitors in a normal room, you've probably heard it: one bass note that booms while others disappear. That's not your speakers. It's your room.

Unboom finds that note and turns just that part down:

Sit where you normally listen
Let it scan with your Mac's mic (or tap "That's the boom" by ear)
Pick Gentle, Medium, or Strong
Flip Correction On/Off and hear the difference
After that it sits in your menu bar and corrects all Mac audio on those speakers. Each room remembers its speakers, headphones are left alone, it never boosts, and nothing is saved or sent.

Free download with a 14-day trial, then a one-time $19.99 launch price (regular $29.99). Scans are always free.

I'd love to hear what your room sounds like before and after. 🙏

"never boosts" is the detail that makes this trustworthy instead of just another EQ preset, cutting one resonant note is a lot safer than anything that pushes gain elsewhere and risks clipping or exciting a different mode. question on the mic scan: if I move the desk or swap speakers, does it know to prompt a rescan, or is it on me to remember that the room's acoustic signature just changed and go redo it manually.

Never boosts" is the right call - most room correction tools make things worse by pushing up the nulls. How does the mic scan cope with a laptop's built-in mic, which rolls off right where the problem frequencies are? And does the correction apply system-wide or per output device?
This could be really useful for people working with music in small home studios where proper acoustic treatment isn't practical.

name: DevTerminal
tagline: A macOS terminal with a Run button that knows your project
description: DevTerminal is a normal macOS terminal (your shell, your config) where every tab knows what project it's in. ⌘R in an Android app installs it on your phone and streams logcat. In an iOS app it launches in the Simulator or on your iPhone. Spring Boot, Next.js, Flutter, React Native, Rust, Go, Django, Rails and more just work. Run output sits under your shell, so Claude Code keeps the tab. $39 once, no subscription.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt 👋 I'm Nayan.

I build an iOS app, its Android version, a Spring Boot backend and a couple of Next.js sites, mostly on my own. Every morning that meant Xcode, Android Studio, IntelliJ and VS Code open at once, mostly so I could press Run in each one. And these days Claude Code writes a lot of my code in a terminal anyway.

So I built DevTerminal: a normal macOS terminal (your shell, your config) where every tab knows what project it's in, and has a Run button.

• Android: ⌘R builds, installs on your phone or emulator, launches the app and streams logcat. You can install emulators from a menu without opening Android Studio.
• iOS: builds and launches in the Simulator or on your iPhone, with the console attached.
• Spring Boot, Next.js, Node, Flutter, React Native, Rust, Go, Django, Rails, .NET: it finds the right command. Anything else gets a one-line .devterminal.json.
• Run output goes to a panel under your shell, with find and filter, so Claude Code keeps the tab and the logs stay in view.
• Chrome-style tabs, one per project, and Xcode's keys: ⌘R run, ⌘B build, ⌘U test.

It doesn't replace the toolchains. Xcode and the Android SDK still do the building. It replaces opening four IDEs to use them.

🎁 Product Hunt offer: 20% off this week with code PRODUCTHUNT. $39 once, no subscription, 14-day refund.

What should Run support next? I'm around all day to answer questions.

the pitch holds up right until the moment you need to set a breakpoint. for a lot of people the reason the four IDEs stay open isn't the run button, it's that occasionally you need to stop execution and inspect a variable, and that's a debugger attached to the build, not a shell your run output lands in. when that moment hits, does DevTerminal hand off to lldb/jdb in a usable way, or is pulling up the real IDE still part of the workflow for that one case? if it's the latter, the honest claim is closer to "skip the IDE for most of your run cycles" rather than "replace the IDEs," which is still a real win, just a narrower one than the headline suggests.

name: FloorGen
tagline: Draw the house, or just ask. Free floor plans with AI
description: Plan a remodel, an ADU or a whole house for free in your browser. Describe it and FloorGen AI builds it, every change an undo step. Then check it against the IRC, walk through it in 3D and print the plan set. Claude and ChatGPT can edit it too.

nodes.body:
Hey everyone, Vinit here.

Floor plan tools usually make you pick: easy and rough, or precise and slow. FloorGen tries to be both, and now you can just ask.

1. Draw: feet and inches to 1/16″, live dimensions, 27 templates.
2. Ask: tell FloorGen AI what you want. It proposes a plan, builds it, and checks its own work. Every change can be undone, and it stops to ask before deleting anything.
3. Check: IRC checks as you draw (plus Canada, UK, Germany and Mexico City profiles), and "Fix with AI" on each issue.
4. Walk through: every plan is a furnished 3D model, day or night.
5. Print: elevations and plan sets to scale, as PDF, DXF, SVG or glTF.

For AI folks: Claude, ChatGPT and Cursor connect over MCP (149 tools), and their edits land live in the editor you have open.

Designing needs no account; FloorGen AI and sync need a free sign-in. Everything is free right now. Tell me what breaks and what you'd want next. I'm here all day.

floorgen.app
Every plan I've got for a unit is an old scan of the whole floor, and the apartment is just one piece of it. How does the trace deal with pulling a single unit out?

the IRC check is the feature I'd be most careful about trusting. passing the base IRC doesn't mean a plan is permit ready, most cities and counties layer local amendments on top (setbacks, egress rules, sometimes stricter stair or ceiling height requirements) and those vary block by block in some places. "fix with AI" on an IRC issue is useful for catching the obvious stuff, but is there anything telling a user their specific jurisdiction needs a human stamp before this goes anywhere near a permit office?

The idea is simple: slide one finger up along the physical edge of your trackpad to increase the volume, or down to decrease it. Thanks for giving it a try! Links - Website: edgevolume.vercel.app - Source: https://github.com/reveuse12/edg...

name: Pickle Sensei
tagline: AI pickleball coach for solo practice, one swing at a time
description: Pickle Sensei turns solo pickleball practice into a clear feedback loop. Step into the start zone, swing one stroke, and get an estimated player rating, technique score, checkpoint scores, and the one thing to fix next. Train serves, returns, drives, dinks, third-shot drops, volleys, and overheads with slow-motion skeleton review, 40+ drills, progress tracking, and ranks. Video stays on your device. Try one rating free, then Pro from $7.99/month.

nodes.body:
Hey Product Hunt! I'm Raunak, the solo developer behind Pickle Sensei.

I play a lot of pickleball, and the hardest part of improving was knowing what I was actually doing wrong. Lessons are expensive and filming yourself doesn't tell you much on its own.

So I built a coach that lives on your phone. You set it up side-on, step into frame on your own, hit a stroke, and on-device pose tracking measures your form. Instead of a wall of stats, you get a score and one clear fix to work on next, plus a slow-mo replay that pauses at each key phase. It's built for solo practice, not for filming games.

A few things I cared about:

  • Privacy: your video never leaves your phone.

  • - Honesty: ratings are coaching estimates, not official ratings, and a failed scan never uses your free rating.

  • - Fast: no shot picker or timer. It detects the stroke and stops on its own.

It's free to try with one rating, and Pro unlocks unlimited. I'll be here all day answering questions.

one side-on camera is a real constraint for pickleball specifically, a lot of what separates a good dink from a bad one is paddle face angle and wrist position at contact, which a silhouette view from the side can hide or guess wrong on. the "honesty" framing in your post is the right instinct, so does the technique score account for what the single angle genuinely can't see, or is there a risk it confidently scores a stroke well when the real fault was never visible to the camera in the first place?

name: Farol
tagline: The macOS terminal that shows which coding agent needs you
description: Farol is a macOS terminal for running Claude Code and Codex in parallel. A sidebar shows which agent is working, which is waiting for you and which is done, and the menu bar shows it from any app. Each task gets its own git worktree, started from a prompt, a GitHub issue or a Jira ticket. Review the diff, commit, push and open the PR in the same window. Built on libghostty, so it reads your Ghostty config. Free and MIT licensed. No account, no telemetry.

nodes.body:
Hi Product Hunt, I'm Lucas, the maker of Farol.

I run three or four Claude Code and Codex sessions at once, and I kept cycling through tabs to find the one stuck on a permission prompt. Farol is the terminal I built to stop doing that. The name is Portuguese for lighthouse.

Each session has a dot in the sidebar: working, waiting for you, or done. The same state shows in the menu bar or at the notch, so I can be in another app and still see when an agent needs me.

Farol doesn't wrap the agents. Claude Code and Codex run as they do in any terminal and report their state through their own hooks, which you turn on with one click.

A few other things it does:

- New task: describe it, or pick a GitHub issue or Jira ticket. It opens a git worktree on a new branch and starts the agent with the task as its first prompt.
- Review: everything the session changed as one diff, then commit, push and open the PR.
- Conflicts: a three-column merge view when a rebase or merge stops.

The terminal is libghostty, the engine behind Ghostty, so it renders like Ghostty and reads your Ghostty config. The app around it is native Swift. It's free, MIT licensed, with no account and no telemetry.

It's early, and Apple Silicon with macOS 14 or later only. I use it as my daily terminal, but expect rough edges.

How do you keep track of several agents today? I'd like to know what you'd want from a terminal built for it.

separate worktrees solves the file-conflict half of running agents in parallel, but not the half that actually bites me: two tasks that touch the same API contract or shared schema from different worktrees, where neither agent can see the other's change until someone opens both diffs side by side at merge time. does Farol do anything to flag "these two active tasks touched overlapping files or symbols" before you're staring at a nasty rebase, or is that still on the human to catch by reading both PRs?

name: NotchPit

nodes.body:
Hi Product Hunt 👋

I built NotchPit because the notch on my MacBook was just… a notch. I kept switching windows to skip a song, check the next prayer time, or see if my site was still up.

NotchPit turns that space into a control center you arrange yourself:

• 64 extensions you turn on only if you want them: notes, tasks, weather, currency, file shelf, and for builders uptime & SSL checks, Polar revenue, Google Analytics, App Store and Play Console stats, GitHub, GitLab and Jira
• New in 1.1: drag cards into any order, resize them, swipe through carousel rows, and pull the notch down to open it

It's a native SwiftUI app for Apple Silicon Macs on macOS 14+, and it works on displays without a notch too. It asks for a permission only when you turn on the feature that needs it, and API keys stay in your Mac's Keychain.

Pricing is simple: 14 days free with no account or card, then one payment for a lifetime license, with a 14-day refund window.

What would you put in your notch? I'm here all day to answer questions.
